title: Bidirectional BFS in Altona: Two-Way Speedrun!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS race across Hamburg’s Altona street graph by searching simultaneously from start and goal until the frontiers meet. The moment the paths touch, the shortest route snaps into view—efficient, visual, and grounded in real-world navigation graphs.
ig_caption:
🚦✨ **Bidirectional BFS** in **Hamburg (Altona)** is like having two teams sprint from opposite ends of a map—until they shake hands. 

🧠 **What you’re seeing (deep technical):** Bidirectional BFS runs BFS from **source** and **target** in parallel on an unweighted graph. Each step expands the frontier one edge at a time, which guarantees the first meeting point yields a **shortest path** in terms of number of edges. 

🌍 **Real-map framing:** Treat city streets as a graph: intersections are **nodes**, road segments are **edges**. On dense urban layouts, bidirectional search can dramatically reduce explored nodes compared to one-way BFS by shrinking the effective search radius. 

📉 **Why it’s fast:** In typical graphs, BFS explores level-by-level; doing it from both ends replaces exploring ~b^d with roughly ~2·b^(d/2) (conceptually), where b is branching factor and d is solution depth. 

👉 Want a version with weighted roads (Dijkstra/A*) next? Drop a 🔥 and comment your favorite city district for the next visualization!
fb_caption:
Hamburg (Altona) street network turned into a graph—and **Bidirectional BFS** shows how graph search can find the shortest route fast. By expanding BFS from both the start and destination simultaneously, we meet in the middle and reconstruct the optimal path.

yt_description:

Watch how two BFS frontiers expand level-by-level, meet in the middle, and reconstruct the shortest path in an unweighted graph.
